This queue is not moving at all. Is the coffee worth it?
Honestly, no. But I am staying anyway. I am Ingrid, from Munich.
Dejair, from Brazil. What are you working on at the moment?
Nerve damage in diabetes. We are collecting data in four hospitals until December. And you?
I work on nerve damage too, but caused by leprosy.
Leprosy? Really. Say that again, I am not sure I heard it right.
Leprosy. The infection is treated, and the pain stays. It is the same problem as yours, from another cause.
That is exactly the connection I am looking for. Are you presenting this week?
Not this time. But can we exchange contact details? Here is my card.
Thank you. I will follow up next week and send you our protocol.

I have to go, but I will follow up next week.

I am Ingrid Vogel and I work at a university in Munich. Can I tell you the only thing I know about congresses? Nobody is comfortable. The people standing alone with a coffee are not unfriendly. They are waiting for somebody to speak first, exactly like you. In my first years I stood at the side of the room and I told myself that my English was not good enough. Then a colleague told me something I still use. She said: do not prepare a speech, prepare one question. You are not going there to perform. You are going there to ask. Now I approach two or three people every day at a congress, and I always start with the same sentence. What are you working on at the moment?

Dejair, it is Ayse. We are all in the coffee area on the first floor and I am looking at you from here, standing alone by the window with your phone. Come over. There are four of us and two of them work on nerve damage, so this is your table, not mine. Bring your phone, but put it in your pocket. One more thing, and then I stop. Do not say sorry for your English before you speak. I did that for years. People do not hear the mistake, they hear the apology, and then they think you are not sure about your science either. You are not here as a student of English. You are here as a researcher.
